title: let your guest be as a god
hookLine: a knock on Diwali night, and a line that says the guest is a god
carry: the guest is honored as a god
tomorrow: where are you really from? what does an old verse say?
last: THE RIVER COMES TO THE CUP.

lines: IS IT OKAY THAT WE CAME?
cards: The doorbell goes in the middle of the puja. Diwali night on an ordinary street: clay lamps along one front window, and every other house dark, because for the rest of the block it's a regular weeknight.
On the step stand the neighbors from across the road, holding a plate of store-bought cookies, a little unsure. We saw the lights, they say. Is it okay that we came?
Behind the door, the family looks at each other. The prayers aren't finished. The sweets are counted.
Nobody has ever knocked on Diwali before.

teach.b: The father opens the door wide, and an old line explains why. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad. At the end of their studies, a teacher gives students parting words for the life ahead.
Among them, in paraphrase: let your mother be as a god to you. Let your father be as a god. Let your teacher be as a god.
Let your guest be as a god. In Sanskrit, that last one is atithi devo bhava. The stories show what it looks like.
In the Bhagavata Purana, a poor brahmin named Sudama walks to the golden city of Dvaraka to see his boyhood friend Krishna, now a king.
All he can bring is a handful of flattened rice tied in a cloth, and he's ashamed of it.
Krishna sees him, rises from his seat, embraces him, washes his dusty feet, and eats the rice as if it were a feast.

God himself plays the host, and treats the guest as holy. That's a real Hindu teaching, and many families still live it: the guest is honored as a god, and is often fed first. And the line sets no conditions.
Not if the guest shares your faith, or brought the right gift. Now carry it across an ocean. A family in the diaspora starts out as the newcomers.
Years later they're the hosts, and the neighbors are the ones unsure on the step. So the cookies go on the table beside the sweets, and each visitor gets a small clay lamp to light.

how: Hindu families outside India sometimes open their homes at Diwali to neighbors and friends of any background, sharing sweets and lamps, in the spirit of 'atithi devo bhava'.

let your guest be as a god
the guest's company in the line

s: the Upanishad honors a guest only if they share the family's faith
it just says the guest. no conditions on who the guest is.
in the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna washes the feet of his poor friend Sudama
and eats Sudama's handful of rice like a feast. the guest is holy.
atithi devo bhava is only a modern slogan, not an old text
it's from the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher's parting words to students.

games.q: a coworker who just moved to town eats lunch alone, and your family's festival dinner is this weekend. what fits the Upanishad's parting words?
o: wait until he's been around long enough to feel like family.
invite him. the guest stands beside mother, father and teacher.
leave it. a festival dinner is for people who share it.
games.why: the teacher's parting words put the guest in the same row as mother, father and teacher, with no conditions about who the guest is.

practice: Say the line softly, a piece at a time: atithi, devo, bhava. As you say it, bring to mind someone who once arrived in your life as a stranger, at a door, a desk or a table.
Hold their face for the rest of the sit, as a guest worth honoring.

wordCard.voice: The diaspora: Hindu families far from the lands of their stories, newcomers who in time become the hosts.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: let your guest be as a god.

carryVoice: Your line: the guest is honored as a god. Mother, father, teacher, guest. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (the teacher's parting instruction: let your mother, father, teacher and guest each be as a god to you)
Bhagavata Purana 10.80–81 (Sudama visits Krishna at Dvaraka; Krishna embraces him, washes his feet and eats his flattened rice)
